question: Citizens have a democratic right to know their country’s past, including periods of totalitarian rule, and how foreign powers sought to control their societies. This right is rooted in Articles 2 and 10(3) of the Treaty on European Union and Articles 8(2) and 11(1) of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights.

Parliament called for these archives to be opened in its resolution of 2 April 2009 on European conscience and totalitarianism1. This is shared European history; opening the archives ensures it is neither forgotten nor distorted. Germany opened the Stasi records in 1991, the Baltic states have opened their KGB files, and on 4 November 2026 Hungary made its state-security archive searchable online.

In several Member States, Finland included, comparable material remains closed at the holding agency’s discretion, some until 2050. Countries that have experienced methods used by authoritarian regimes in the past to erode societies – methods also used by Russia today – should open their archives to help counter such erosion in the future. 1.
Will the Commission, under the European Democracy Shield, propose common principles for opening Cold War intelligence records, based on existing national models?
Will it fund digitisation and cross-border research access (under the Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV) programme and Horizon Europe)?
Will it treat archive openness as part of democratic resilience in the Rule of Law Report?
OJ C 137 E, 27.5.2010, p. 25.
